Weight-for-height Z-score in Bangladeshi infants aged 6-13 months

Dataset 7: Bangladesh growth monitoring and promotion survey

RSR feasibility analysis

2026-08-03

Introduction

The data come from a cross-sectional household survey in rural Bangladesh that compared two ways of delivering growth monitoring and promotion (GMP): sessions held at a community clinic (“facility-based”) and sessions held in the community/home (“home-based”). Caregivers of 3038 young children across six upazilas were interviewed and the children were weighed and measured (source paper: PLOS ONE, e0324918). Weight-for-height Z-score (WHZ) captures acute undernutrition — thinness relative to length — and is the index most responsive to recent food shortage and illness, so in principle it is the outcome most likely to move on a short timescale in response to a programme.

Aim. Among rural Bangladeshi infants aged 6-13 months, we examined which of GMP delivery model, child sex, child age, mother’s age, mother’s schooling, household asset tertile, NGO membership and toilet quality are independently associated with weight-for-height Z-score, mutually adjusting for the others.

This is a Purpose 3 analysis: several predictors are of interest and the question is which remain associated with the outcome after mutual adjustment.

Methods

Data source. Cross-sectional survey of 3038 caregiver-child pairs in six rural upazilas of Bangladesh. The study sampled 60 community-clinic catchment areas, arranged as matched pairs, one area of each pair receiving facility-based and the other home-based GMP. The file supplied for this catalogue contains one row per child.

Variables. The outcome is weight_for_height_z, the WHO weight-for-height Z-score in standard-deviation units; more negative values mean thinner children for their length. Predictors are: GMP delivery model (facility-based = reference, home-based); child sex (male = reference); child age in months (continuous, observed range 6.0 to 13.0); mother’s age in years (continuous); mother’s completed schooling in years (continuous); household asset index tertile (lowest = reference, middle, highest); NGO membership (no = reference); and improved toilet facility (no = reference).

Delivery model versus sub-district. delivery_model and sub_district are almost the same variable: only 8 of 3038 records (0.3%) sit in a sub-district whose other children received the alternative model. Fitting both together yields variance inflation factors of roughly 96 and 103 and inflates the delivery-model standard error about nine-fold, with the coefficient flipping sign. We kept delivery_model, the substantive programme exposure the survey was built around, and excluded sub_district. Genuine geographic differences between the six upazilas are therefore absorbed into the delivery-model coefficient and cannot be distinguished from it — a point that matters unusually much for this outcome, because delivery model is the one predictor that changes status after adjustment.

Near-constant variables dropped. mother_occupation is 97.5% “housewife” and religion_muslim is 97.8% Muslim; both were left out of the main model and are shown in a sensitivity fit in the feasibility notes.

Other Z-scores excluded. weight_for_age_z and height_for_age_z are not predictors. Weight-for-height is computed from the same weight and length measurements, so regressing it on either is an arithmetic exercise, not an epidemiological one.

Statistical analysis. Linear regression via lm(), justified because the outcome is a continuous, approximately symmetric Z-score. We fitted a univariable model for each predictor first, then a single multivariable model containing all of them. Predictors were chosen in advance on subject-matter grounds, not by significance. Significance threshold 0.05; estimates are reported with 95% confidence intervals. Assumptions were checked with performance::check_model(). Analysis used R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24) with tidyverse, gtsummary and performance.

Missing data. Complete-case analysis: 3031 of 3038 rows were analysed (7 dropped).

Median weight-for-height Z-score is -0.50, only about half a standard deviation below the WHO reference median, and 7.2% of children fall at or below the -2 wasting threshold. This is a far less shifted distribution than height-for-age in the same children, which is the expected pattern: chronic deficits accumulate, acute ones do not.

Exploratory figure

Figure 1. Weight-for-height Z-score against child age, by growth-monitoring delivery model. Points are individual children; lines are loess smooths with 95% confidence bands; the dashed line marks the -2 wasting threshold.

Weight-for-height declines steadily across the narrow 6-13-month window in both arms, with the home-based curve sitting slightly below the facility-based one throughout — a small and roughly constant gap rather than a divergence.

Unadjusted, household wealth is again the strongest correlate: children in the highest asset tertile score 0.334 (95% CI 0.239 to 0.429) Z-units above the lowest tertile (p < 0.001). Each additional year of maternal schooling is associated with 0.040 (95% CI 0.029 to 0.050) (p < 0.001) — noticeably weaker than the same slope for height-for-age, consistent with education acting mainly on chronic rather than acute deficit. Weight-for-height falls with child age (-0.073 (95% CI -0.095 to -0.051) per month, p < 0.001) and with mother’s age (-0.013 (95% CI -0.020 to -0.006), p < 0.001). The programme variable sits exactly on the conventional threshold: children in home-based areas score -0.078 (95% CI -0.156 to 0.000) relative to facility-based areas (p = 0.051). Child sex (p = 0.164), NGO membership (p = 0.159) and improved toilet (p = 0.087) are not significant crude.

Why adjustment is needed

Household asset tertile is the dominant confounder in this dataset. It predicts maternal schooling, latrine ownership and NGO membership on one side, and food security and illness exposure — hence weight-for-height — on the other, so every socio-economic crude estimate here is partly a wealth estimate. Mother’s schooling confounds in the reverse direction: better-educated mothers live in wealthier households, so the crude asset gradient contains an education component. Improved toilet facility is a third: sanitation is concentrated in wealthier households (93% coverage overall) and poor sanitation causes the diarrhoeal illness that produces acute weight loss, so its crude coefficient cannot be interpreted without holding wealth constant. Child age must be adjusted for on structural grounds, because weight-for-height declines appreciably even over the seven months observed here. Adjustment matters particularly for the delivery-model comparison: although the study allocated delivery models to matched-pair areas, the two arms are not perfectly balanced on asset tertile (the highest tertile is slightly over-represented in home-based areas), so the crude programme contrast carries a wealth imbalance with it.

The model explains only 4.2% of the variance in weight-for-height (adjusted R-squared 0.039) — the weakest fit of the three Z-score outcomes, which fits the interpretation that acute thinness is driven by short-term shocks that this survey did not measure. Holding the other predictors constant, children in the highest asset tertile score 0.259 (95% CI 0.158 to 0.360) above the lowest (p < 0.001); each extra year of maternal schooling adds 0.028 (95% CI 0.016 to 0.040) (p < 0.001); and each additional month of age is associated with -0.073 (95% CI -0.095 to -0.051) (p < 0.001). Adjusted for household circumstances, children in home-based GMP areas score -0.090 (95% CI -0.171 to -0.008) relative to facility-based areas (p = 0.032). That result should be treated with considerable caution — see the limitations on clustering below.

The interesting movement here runs in both directions. One predictor moved away from the null and gained significance: the home-based versus facility-based difference went from -0.078 (95% CI -0.156 to 0.000) (p = 0.051) to -0.090 (95% CI -0.171 to -0.008) (p = 0.032). This is negative confounding: home-based areas contain slightly wealthier households, which was masking a small deficit, and holding wealth constant unmasks it. Two predictors moved toward the null and lost significance. Maternal schooling attenuated from 0.040 (95% CI 0.029 to 0.050) to 0.028 (95% CI 0.016 to 0.040), a 30% reduction (still significant); mother’s age went from -0.013 (95% CI -0.020 to -0.006) (p < 0.001) to -0.007 (95% CI -0.014 to 0.000) (p = 0.057); and the middle-versus-lowest asset contrast lost significance, 0.126 (95% CI 0.031 to 0.220) (p = 0.009) to 0.089 (95% CI -0.005 to 0.184) (p = 0.064). Improved toilet collapsed to nothing, from 0.137 (95% CI -0.020 to 0.294) to -0.002 (95% CI -0.160 to 0.156) — its crude association was entirely a wealth proxy. Child sex and child age barely moved (age -0.073 (95% CI -0.095 to -0.051) to -0.073 (95% CI -0.095 to -0.051), sex -0.056 (95% CI -0.134 to 0.023) to -0.058 (95% CI -0.135 to 0.018)), as expected for variables not determined by household circumstances. None of this is collinearity: all variance inflation factors are under 1.3.

The posterior predictive check reproduces the observed weight-for-height distribution well. Linearity is satisfied — the residual smooth is flat, so linear terms for age and schooling are adequate. Homogeneity of variance holds across the fitted range. The normality of residuals Q-Q plot is close to the line through the body of the distribution with modest departure in both tails, partly reflecting the severe-malnutrition exclusion truncating the left tail and a few implausibly high Z-scores (above +4) on the right; neither threatens inference at this sample size. No observation crosses the Cook’s-distance contours in the influential observations panel. Collinearity is fine as specified, but only because sub_district was deliberately excluded.

Discussion

Among rural Bangladeshi infants aged 6-13 months, acute undernutrition as measured by weight-for-height is only weakly patterned by the household characteristics recorded in this survey. Household wealth and maternal schooling retain independent associations after mutual adjustment; sanitation, maternal age and NGO membership do not. The one result that changes status on adjustment is the programme comparison: home-based GMP areas show a small deficit in weight-for-height once household wealth is held constant. Given the design, this should be read as a hypothesis and not as evidence that home-based delivery harms children.

Limitations.

Clustering cannot be modelled, and this outcome is where that bites hardest. Delivery model is an area-level exposure assigned to whole upazilas — six of them — with 60 community-clinic catchment areas sampled as matched pairs. Children in the same catchment share fieldworkers, scales, clinics and food markets, so their weight-for-height values are correlated. The file carries no clinic or cluster identifier, so no random effect or cluster-robust standard error is possible. The nominally significant adjusted delivery-model result (p = 0.032) rests on a standard error computed as though 3031 children were independent when the effective number of independent units is closer to 60, or arguably six. Even a modest design effect would push that interval back across zero. sub_district is not a usable substitute cluster variable because it is collinear with the exposure. This single result should not be reported as a finding.

The outcome distribution is truncated by design. The source paper states that children with severe stunting, wasting or underweight were excluded on ethical grounds so they could be referred for treatment. Yet the shipped file contains 26 children with weight-for-height below -3 and 203 with height-for-age below -3, so the exclusion was incomplete or applied on some other criterion. The lower tail of weight-for-height has therefore been interfered with: the 7.2% wasting prevalence observed here understates the true burden, and coefficients describing movement into the thinnest part of the distribution are attenuated.

Age definition is inconsistent in the source. The paper’s abstract says children “under one year”, its methods say 6-23 months, and the data run 6.0 to 13.0 months. We describe the observed range only.

Design and residual confounding. Cross-sectional data give associations, not effects. Weight-for-height is the index most sensitive to recent events — diarrhoea in the last fortnight, a seasonal food gap, a feeding interruption — and none of these were recorded. Season of measurement is also unavailable, which matters because wasting in Bangladesh is strongly seasonal. Adjusted R-squared of 0.039 is the honest consequence.

Sparse and dropped variables. mother_occupation and religion_muslim were excluded as near-constant.

Future work. Repeated measurement across seasons, with cluster identifiers and recent-illness histories, would be needed before any statement about GMP delivery and acute undernutrition could be taken seriously.

Feasibility notes

Not part of a student report.

Verdict: usable but the weakest of the three continuous outcomes, and it contains a booby trap. The model fits without complaint, but two things make it harder to supervise than height-for-age or weight-for-age.

  1. The delivery-model result is a trap, not a finding. It is the only place in the whole dataset where the programme exposure crosses p = 0.05, and it does so only after adjustment (p = 0.051 crude to p = 0.032 adjusted). A student will seize on it and write “home-based growth monitoring is associated with worse acute nutritional status”. Given 60 unmodellable clusters and six upazilas, that p-value is almost certainly an artefact of ignoring clustering. The brief must pre-warn markers and students alike.

  2. Weakest fit of the six outcomes. Adjusted R-squared 0.039, and only three predictors reach significance. There is a real risk of a “nothing happened” report.

  3. delivery_model versus sub_district. 99.7% overlap (8 discordant records out of 3038); together they give VIFs of roughly 96 and

    1. Must be chosen between.

  4. Do not put other anthropometry on the right-hand side. weight_for_age_z shares the same weight measurement as this outcome and height_for_age_z/stunted share the same length measurement; any of them as a predictor turns the model into an identity check. A derived wasting indicator is exactly weight_for_height_z <= -2 and must never appear as a predictor here.

  5. Near-constant predictors. Sensitivity fit adding them back:

  1. Overlap with the wasting analysis. Same measurement, dichotomised. The continuous version is strictly more powerful; a student choosing wasting instead should know they are giving up power for interpretability.
